questions.question: A scale of 1 : 50 000 means:
options: One unit on the map represents 50 000 of the same unit on the ground
One centimetre on the map represents 50 000 km
Fifty thousand maps fit into the real area

questions.question: A route measuring 7 cm on a 1 : 50 000 map has a real length of:
The three steps of the number-scale method, in order, are:
options: Measure the map distance, multiply by the scale number, convert to sensible units

subtopics.title: Bar Scales and the Photocopier Problem

questions.question: A bar scale is:
options: A printed bar whose segments are labelled with the real distance each represents
A list of towns and distances
The north arrow of the map

questions.question: If 2 cm of bar represents 10 km, a road measuring 9 cm on the map is:
After a map is photocopied smaller, the bar scale still works because:
options: The photocopier corrects the ratio automatically
Bar scales are printed in special ink
The bar shrinks along with the roads, so the proportion between bar and route survives
The bar scale was never accurate to begin with

questions.question: The trade-off between the two scale types is:
options: Bar scales are exact; number scales are rough
Number scales only work in kilometres
The number scale is exact but only true at original size; the bar scale is robust to resizing but inherits measuring error

questions.question: A grid reference like B3 locates:
options: The block where column B crosses row 3, not the exact doorstep
An exact point accurate to the metre
The distance from the map edge

Left and right differ from compass directions because they:
options: Depend on which way the traveller is facing

subtopics.title: The Map Shrinks the World Evenly

questions.question: The 'evenness' of a map's shrinking matters because:
options: Anything measured on the paper can be multiplied back up to the real distance
Only main roads are drawn to scale
It lets the map ignore units

questions.question: Tidying 350 000 cm into sensible units gives:
The sense test for scale calculations says:
options: Both directions should give similar numbers
Map answers are always in kilometres
Paper to world must grow much bigger; world to paper must shrink much smaller
Dividing is always safer than multiplying

subtopics.title: The Little Bar That Survives the Photocopier

questions.question: If one bar stripe of 2 cm represents 10 km, then one centimetre of map means:
Measuring a route with no ruler can be done by:
options: Ticking the route on a paper edge and counting stripes against the bar

questions.question: After shrinking a map on a photocopier, the printed ratio 1 : 50 000:
options: Adjusts itself to the new size
No longer tells the truth, because one centimetre of the copy covers a different real distance
Applies only to the bar scale

questions.question: The bar scale's weakness is that:
options: It only works on road maps
It is always less honest than the ratio
You measure the bar itself, so the answer inherits your ruler and your eye

subtopics.title: Getting There: Blocks, Turns and Petrol Money

questions.question: A full-marks route description contains:
options: Street names, turn directions and a landmark to confirm arrival
The scale and the grid letters

questions.question: Walking south down a street, west is:
options: On your right — turning the map around in your head prevents the flip

questions.question: The 18 km trip at 60 km/h takes 18 minutes, not 30, because:
options: The taxi is faster than the car
The map scale changes the time
0,3 of an hour is 0,3 × 60 = 18 minutes — decimal hours are not minutes

questions.question: For four people travelling together, car against taxi works out as:
options: Car cheaper — R67,68 altogether against R208 by taxi, a saving of R140,32
